t: whether testimony by which he would obligate his fellow. That would confirm the plaintiff's claim.
or testimony by which he would acquit him. That would confirm the defendant's claim.

and this is provided that he demands him to testify in monetary cases. In monetary cases the obligation to testify applies only if one of the litigants demanded that he testify. By contrast, in capital cases, lashes and the like, he must come on his own to testify even if they did not demand it of him (see Kesef Mishneh and below, halacha 2; and see Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:3).

as it is said, "and he is a witness" etc.. The obligation to testify mentioned at the beginning of the halacha is derived from the sense of the verse "and he is a witness... if he does not tell, he shall bear his iniquity." Although the verse there is interpreted as referring to one who knows testimony and swears falsely that he does not know, who becomes liable for a sliding-scale offering for this oath (see Hilchot Shevuot 1:12), nevertheless the verse's meaning also includes the obligation itself to testify (see Yad Peshutah).

the commandment of honoring the Torah takes precedence. The commandment to be careful with the honor of a Torah scholar (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:1) is more important and takes precedence over the commandment to testify.
and he may refrain. He is permitted to refrain, and is not obliged to forgo his honor.
but with testimony by which he separates from a prohibition. For example, testifying about a woman whose absent husband is alive and she is forbidden to remarry.
and likewise in capital or corporal cases. Testifying in cases whose penalty is death or lashes.

wherever there is a desecration of the Name. That if he does not testify, people will not know to refrain from the prohibition, or transgressors will not be punished, and the Name of Heaven will be desecrated.
the High Priest is not obligated to testify. For it is not in keeping with his honor to come to court to testify (see also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:9).
except for testimony concerning the king of Israel. That concerns the king.
to inquire of the witnesses. Exactly how the act itself happened.
and to examine them. Where and when exactly the act was done.
and they remove. They move aside.
so that they will be silent. So that they will not know how to answer.
a flaw. A defect.
and the judges must be careful. In phrasing their questions to the witnesses.
lest from them they learn to lie. Lest from the questions the judges ask them, the witnesses learn details known to the court, and it will be easy for them to lie.
in which shevu'a. In which Shemittah cycle of the Jubilee cycles the event took place.
in which year. Of the years of the Shemittah cycle.

even if he said, "Today he killed him" or "Last night he killed him," they ask him etc.. So that for the purpose of establishing the facts there is no longer any place to ask them "in which shevu'a," "in which year," etc.; nevertheless they ask them again in order to increase the questioning and burden them, so that if there is falsehood in their testimony they will retract (Peirush HaMishnayot, Sanhedrin 5:1).

and among the examinations, more than the seven that apply in everything etc.. Besides the seven examinations of witnesses that apply to any testimony whatsoever, the examination of witnesses also includes questions that deal with clarifying the act itself (and these questions are called derishah; see below, halacha 6, 2:1, 3:3).
that if they testified against him that he worshiped idols, they ask them what he worshiped. Which idol he worshiped.
and in which manner he worshiped. In what way he worshiped it.
the intent of the act that he performed. Precise clarification of the act itself, through the inquiry of the witnesses.
and fixing the time and fixing the place. Precise clarification of the time and place at which the act was done, through the examination of the witnesses.
in which the witnesses may be refuted by hazamah or not. For only after the time and place are clarified is it possible for other witnesses to refute the witnesses (see below 18:2).
for we cannot refute the witnesses until they fix the time and the place. And it is a rule that any testimony that cannot be refuted is not testimony (see Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 41a).
stalks. The tail of the fruit, the part that connects it to the tree.

What is the difference between examinations and checks. The examination of witnesses includes the seven examinations in which the witnesses are asked exactly where and when the act was done, and the inquiry of the witnesses with questions that deal with clarifying the act itself (as explained above 1:4). The checks are additional questions asked of the witnesses on matters that are not the essence of the testimony (there, halacha 6). Here the halachic difference between these types of questions is explained.
if one fixed his testimony. He clarified his testimony precisely.
and the second witness said, "I do not know". And did not testify precisely where, when or how the act occurred.

their testimony is void. Since without clarification of the act itself there is no testimony at all, and even clarification of the time and place of the act is required for the testimony to stand, because without it the witnesses cannot be refuted (there, halacha 5).

but in the checks, even if both say, "We do not know," their testimony stands. Since the checks deal with secondary matters that are not the essence of the testimony, the witnesses may claim they are not familiar with them.
and when they contradict one another. Contradicting each other's words.
in such-and-such shevu'a. In such-and-such Shemittah cycle of the Jubilee cycles.
in such-and-such year. Of the Shemittah years.
on Wednesday. On the fourth day of the week.
with a sword. With a blade.
he fixed his testimony in everything except the hours. He clarified his testimony precisely apart from the hour of the incident.
and I did not notice the weapon that was in his hand. I did not pay attention to the weapon with which he killed.
his clothes. His garments.

their testimony is void etc.. When witnesses contradict each other, even on a secondary matter that is not part of the act itself, the testimony is void, as if they had contradicted each other in the substance of the testimony.
with a sword. With a blade.
with a spear. With a (long) lance.

as it is said, "the matter is established". It says in the verse: "You shall inquire, investigate and ask diligently, and behold, it is true, the matter is established," from which it follows that both testimonies must be precise and consistent, and there must be no contradiction between them.
if the witnesses were many. More than two, for example if three witnesses came to testify.
the testimony stands with the two. For the testimony of the third witness is void because he said "I do not know" (as above, halacha 1).
and he be executed. The one about whom they testified that he killed a person.
but if he contradicted both of them. He contradicted their words in his testimony.
their testimony stands. And the discrepancy between them is not considered a contradiction in their testimony.

for this one knew about the intercalation of the month. That the previous month was full, thirty days, and the current month began only on Tuesday. Therefore he testified that the act, which occurred on Wednesday, was on the second of the month.

and this one did not know. Rather, he thought that the previous month was deficient, twenty-nine days, and the current month began on Monday. Therefore he erred and testified that the act, which occurred on Wednesday, was on the third of the month.
the middle of the month. The mid-point of the month.

for the middle of the month does not arrive until everyone already knows when the new moon was. After half a month has passed everyone already knows when Rosh Chodesh was, and since the matter is known and public to all, the contradiction in their testimony cannot be attributed to an error about the intercalation of the month.

one said on the third of the month and the second says on the fifth, their testimony is void. For when there is a gap of two days between them, the contradiction in their testimony cannot be attributed to an error about the intercalation of the month.
at two hours of the day. At the second hour from the start of the day.
and likewise if they disagreed about its setting. That one testifies that the act was before sunset, and the other testifies that it was after.
with derishah and chakirah. The judges are commanded to examine the witnesses thoroughly and make sure there is no flaw in their testimony (as explained above 1:4).

but the Sages said, so that you do not lock the door before borrowers, witnesses in monetary cases do not require derishah and chakirah. For if the judges had to examine them, the lender would refrain from lending, for fear that the witnesses would err in the examination and he would be unable to collect his debt.
even though they did not fix the month nor the place in which he lent it to him. They did not state precisely the date or the place where the loan was made.

nor the maneh, whether it was of such-and-such coinage or such-and-such coinage. They did not say what kind of coin the maneh he lent him was (for example, whether it was a coin of one country or another, both of the same value, or they did not know whether he lent him one coin worth a maneh or a hundred dinar coins worth a maneh).
in admissions and loans. Where they testify about a person who admitted before them that he owes money to his fellow, or that he borrowed money from him.
in cases of fines. Laws whose penalty is a fine, such as double, fourfold and fivefold payments.
in lashes and exile. Laws whose penalty is lashes or exile.
and likewise if the judge saw that the case is fraudulent and suspected it. That he suspected that the witnesses or the litigants are deceiving (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 24:3).
if the witnesses contradicted one another. They contradicted each other in their testimony.
in chakirot or in derishot. Questions dealing with the time and place of the act ("chakirot") and with clarifying the act itself ("derishot"; see above 1:4).
their testimony is void. Since without clarification of where, when and how it happened, there is no testimony at all.
in the checks. Questions on secondary matters that are not the essence of the testimony (above 1:6).

their testimony stands. Because the witnesses may claim they are not familiar with them (and only in capital cases is there a special teaching that even a contradiction in the checks voids the testimony, as above 2:2).
one says in Nisan... or one said in Jerusalem... their testimony is void. For in these cases they were contradicted in the examination.
a black maneh. One that has darkened with age.
a white maneh. A new one.
an upper story. A floor.
for a maneh is included within two hundred. And therefore this is not considered a contradiction in the essence of the testimony.

and likewise if one said, "He has in his hand the price of a barrel of wine," and this one says, "the price of a barrel of oil". For example, this one says, "In my presence he admitted to him the price of a barrel of wine," and this one says, "In my presence he admitted to him the price of a barrel of oil."
he pays the lesser of the amounts. The lower value of the two, which is included in the two hundred, a maneh.
from the mouth of the witnesses. That they come and state their testimony before the court.
and not from their handwriting. They may not send their testimony in writing.
by rabbinic enactment. An enactment of the Sages.
that they decide. They rule and determine.
on the testimony of a document. On the basis of the witnesses signed on the document.
even though the witnesses are not alive. Because they died or are not available.

so that you do not lock the door before borrowers. For if the testimony in a document were not accepted, lenders would refrain from lending, fearing that after some time it would not be possible to bring the witnesses to testify in court and they would not be able to collect their debt.
I was misled. I was misled in understanding the event.
I was mistaken. I erred in understanding the event.
I did it out of fear of him. I was afraid he would kill me (based on Peirush HaMishnayot, Ketubot 2:3).
we do not listen to him even if he gave a reason for his words. Even if he explained why he wants to retract, he cannot; he may not retract.

and likewise he cannot add a condition to his testimony. To add to his first testimony and testify that the monetary obligation was conditional. For example, he first testified that Reuven sold his house to Shimon, and now says that the sale was on a certain condition and he does not know whether the condition was fulfilled.
and they cannot retract. And testify that what is written in the document is not correct.
to validate the document. To identify that this is indeed the signature of the witnesses and to ratify the document (see below 6:2).
not from their mouths. Without the witnesses themselves coming and confirming their signature.
for example, if there were witnesses there that this is their handwriting. That other witnesses identify that this is their signature.
or if their handwriting came out from another place. That their signatures are found on another document and the signatures can be compared with it (see below there, halacha 3).
We were minors, we were relatives etc.. At the time we signed the document.
these are believed and the document is voided. Just as they are believed that this is their signature, so they are to be believed that their testimony is not valid.
we were disqualified from testimony because of a transgression. When we signed the document we were transgressors whose testimony is invalid.
we took a bribe for this testimony. And we signed the document falsely.

and likewise if they said, "Our words were an amanah". We signed a loan document although there was no loan; rather the borrower wrote a loan document and gave it to the lender and they trusted that he would not use it unless he later borrowed from him.

for one who testifies on an amanah document is like one who testifies falsely. For it is forbidden to sign an amanah document, and therefore they cannot incriminate themselves that they signed something sinful.
a protest was delivered to us concerning it. The seller notified us before the sale that he is being forced to sell against his will, and so the sale does not take effect (see Hilchot Mechirah 10:1).

even though their handwriting comes out from another place, these are believed. And they are not considered as retracting from what they wrote in the document, since their claim does not uproot the document entirely: even if the sale was under duress, the document is still needed in order to recover the sale money by it. Likewise they are not considered as voiding the document after it was validated, for they could write a protest document and invalidate the bill of sale from the outset (Kesef Mishneh).
this document was conditional. The monetary obligation in the document was on a certain condition.
if their handwriting comes out from another place, they are not believed. For since the document can be validated without them, their testimony has ended and they cannot add to it (above, halacha 5).

but if the document can be validated only through their mouths, they are believed. For since we still need their testimony to validate the document, we must also believe their statement that the obligation was conditional.
and we say to the litigants, fulfill the condition and come to court. That is, only when the condition is fulfilled will the obligation take effect and you will be able to claim it.

behold there is one witness here. This document is considered a document with only one witness (the one who says there was no condition), and it obligates the defendant to take an oath by Torah law, as below 5:1 (Lechem Mishneh).
also in monetary cases. As in capital cases.
witnesses are not accepted except in the presence of the litigant. The court does not accept the testimony of witnesses not in the presence of the defendant.

not in the presence of a litigant. Because testimony signed in a document is considered as having been examined in court (above, halacha 6), and validation is required only by rabbinic enactment (Kesef Mishneh). Some explain that the reason is that validation of the document does not relate to the content of the document but only to the identity of those who signed it (Rashba in a responsum, cited in Beit Yosef, Choshen Mishpat 46).

rather, they validate the document, and if he has proof to invalidate it, he may invalidate it. They validate the document immediately, and if he has evidence to invalidate the document, he may bring it afterward.
he takes care of the witnesses until he brings them to court. The duty of bringing the witnesses falls on the plaintiff, since the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow.
for his opponent is mute. For the defendant is a violent person.

we compel his opponent to bring the witnesses himself. Instead of the plaintiff bringing witnesses to obligate the defendant, the defendant must locate witnesses who will testify that he is not liable.
and they must testify as one. One after another at the same session (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:3).

and before one court. They must testify before the same court, and the very judges who received the testimony are the ones who will judge on its basis. But if they testified before one court and then testified the same testimony again before another court, some of the judges of the first court cannot join some of the judges of the second court (compare below, halacha 6).

the one who warned him. The one who warns the transgressor and cautions him against the transgression (and the warner may be one of the witnesses or another person who is not one of the witnesses; see Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:2).
and if they do not see one another. If the two groups of witnesses did not see each other.
and the warner did not join them. If even the warner did not see the two groups of witnesses.
he and they are executed. The transgressor and the conspiring witnesses.
in my presence he admitted to him. He admitted to a person that he owes him.

and the second witness said, "and so I too" etc.. The second witness testifies to an event similar to the one the first testified to ("he lent him" or "he admitted"), but testifies to a different time from what the first testified.
and likewise if one said, "In my presence he lent him," and the second says, "In my presence he admitted to him". For each one testifies to a different event.
and when the second witness comes after some time, they hear his words. Even though he did not testify together with the first witness at the same session.
one witness in writing. Signed on a promissory note.
and one witness orally. Who testifies about the debt.
they combine. To obligate payment (and the law of the debt is like that of an oral loan, so the defendant need not repay it in front of witnesses; see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:1).
and if the one who did not write his testimony said. The witness who testified orally.

I acquired from his hand for this matter. I received a kinyan sudar from the defendant's hand, expressing his full commitment to the debt, and I could sign a promissory note (see there, that when a kinyan is made on a debt a document may be written even if this was not expressly stated).
and this lender did not come and did not ask me to write. And only for that reason I did not write a document for the debt in question.

both combine and it becomes a loan with a document, and he cannot say, "I paid it". It has the law of a documented debt, and he is not believed to claim that he paid the debt unless he brings witnesses to that effect, since one who lends to his fellow with a document must repay in front of witnesses (there).
a court may come to a court and their testimonies combine. The two courts combine and judge together on the basis of the testimonies they heard.

one from each and every court may come and they combine. For example, if the witnesses testified before three courts, and then one judge from each court comes and they join together to judge this case (Kesef Mishneh, and many Rishonim explained so in Bava Batra 165b).

but a witness with the judge before whom the two witnesses testified do not combine. To testify before another court, because they are not testifying about one matter, since the witness testifies that he saw the act, while the judge testifies that he heard testimony about the act.

as we have explained. In the previous halachot, that in monetary cases testimony is combined even if the witnesses saw the event at different times or testified in court at different times or in different ways, and in all these cases each of the witnesses must give complete testimony.

we do not combine the testimony of all three and say, "He has eaten it for three years". When a field is in a person's possession and another who was known as the owner of the field comes and claims that the field is his, if the possessor brings witnesses that he ate the field's produce for three consecutive years, it becomes his possession and he is believed to claim that he bought it or received it from the previous owner even if he brings no proof for his words (Hilchot To'en VeNitan 11:2). Since in the case mentioned here each witness testified to a different year, their testimony does not combine (see also there 15:2).

I saw one hair on the right side of this one. In the pubic area. For a person to be defined as an adult and a man he must be thirteen years old and have two hairs in the pubic area (Hilchot Ishut 2:10).
they decide. They rule.
and from the tradition. The Sages' tradition in expounding the verses.
for he stands to take an oath. Although money is not extracted on the testimony of one witness, his testimony obligates the defendant to take an oath by Torah law.
as we have explained in Hilchot To'en. Hilchot To'en VeNitan 1:1.
as we have explained in their place. Hilchot Sotah 1:14, Hilchot Rotzeach 9:12.
by their own words. By the words of the Sages.
in the testimony of a woman, where he testifies for her that her husband died. And she will be permitted to remarry on his word (see Hilchot Gerushin 12:15-16, 13:28).
a woman and an invalid witness so testify. The testimony of a woman or of an invalid witness is also effective.

for an oath is imposed only on the testimony of a valid witness etc.. One witness obligates an oath only in a case where, if another witness joined him, their testimony would obligate the defendant to pay money.

What are two brothers to do etc.. For relatives are disqualified from testifying together (below 13:1), and it cannot be that because both were present at the event, the entire testimony is disqualified.
the testimony of all of them is void. Even of those who did not intend to testify, since a disqualification was found in the main witnesses (Lechem Mishneh).
one who intends to testify and one who did not intend to testify etc.. Even one who did not intend to testify may testify, and the law is decided on his word.
a document whose witnesses were many. That more than two signed on it.

and the witnesses are not alive so that we can ask them. There is no way to clarify with the witnesses themselves whether all of those signed intended to testify, or whether some signed the document out of honor and the like and not for the sake of testimony.
if there is clear evidence that all of them sat to sign, for they all intended to testify. If it is known that they gathered to sign together, it is evident that their intention was to testify.
and they left room for the great one to sign. Above their signatures, out of respect for him.
the one executed may not instruct in this case. He may not serve as a judge in his case.
and he may not teach concerning him neither merit nor guilt. He may not add words about him and argue for merit or guilt after he finished his testimony.
but in monetary cases a witness may argue for merit and guilt. For the verse excluded only a witness who testified in a case of capital punishment.
he shall not be counted among the judges. He shall not take part in the deliberation of the judges (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 11:8).
and he shall not be made a judge. Certainly he cannot serve as a judge in this case.
but in the matter of their own words. In a matter where by Torah law witnesses are not needed at all, and it was the Sages who required witnesses.
one who brought the get. An agent who brought a get from the husband's country to the wife's country.

and said, "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed". For a get brought from a distant place, the Sages feared there would be difficulty in verifying the witnesses' signatures in case of a challenge by the husband, and so they enacted that the agent who brings the get testify that it was written and signed in his presence, and then it can no longer be challenged as to its validity (Hilchot Gerushin 7:8).

he and two give it to her, and it is as if she took it in court. For the agent's testimony about the validity of the get must be stated before a court (similar to the validation of documents, which must be done before a court; see below 6:1), but since this is a rabbinic enactment it suffices that the agent testify before two and that he himself join them as a judge to validate the get (see Hilchot Gerushin 7:19 and below 7:6).

We have already explained that validation of documents is rabbinic, so that you do not lock the door before borrowers. Above 3:4 it was explained that although by Torah law testimony in a document is not accepted, the Sages enacted that in monetary cases a document is effective and money may be collected on it. This is so that people will not refrain from lending, fearing that they will not be able to bring their witnesses after some time and will not be able to collect their debt. However, to prevent the concern that the document is forged, they enacted that the court ratify the signatures on it and note this in the body of the document (Lechem Mishneh; for the text of the validation see below, halacha 4; for the place of writing the validation in the document see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 27:6).

Nevertheless, documents are validated only by three... because it is a judgment. Although the validation of documents is only a confirmation that the witnesses' signatures on the document are valid, and one might have said that two witnesses to this would suffice, the Sages nevertheless enacted that the document be given the full force of a court ruling, and therefore required three, like any matter of law that must be done by three (Hilchot Sanhedrin 2:10; and see Rashbam, Bava Batra 40a).
Therefore documents are not validated at night. Since it is considered a legal proceeding, and court cases are not judged at night (Hilchot Sanhedrin 3:3).
as we have explained. Ibid., halakhah 4.
that the witnesses sign in their presence. That ideally the signing of the document should take place in the presence of the judges.

and I am a witness to this matter. And I remember the event (for a witness who identifies his signature on a document but does not remember the testimony may not testify to his handwriting, as explained below 8:1).
that their handwriting appears on other documents. As detailed in the next halakhah.
and they compare. They match.
and it appears to them together. That all three judges agree that the handwritings are identical.
from two documents of two fields. Two deeds of sale of fields.

that their owners have eaten the produce for three years, a proper and open usage. That the buyers ate from them with confidence and in public view, without fear that claimants would come to contest the sale.

or from two ketubah documents. Of women who live with their husbands under these ketubot and have no concern that they contain any flaw (Kesef Mishneh; and see Meiri, Ketubot 20a, who explained that it is customary to sign ketubot in public).
and this is on condition that the two documents come from the hands of another. That the documents used for the validation were in the possession of another person.

not from the hands of the one who wishes to validate his document, lest he forged everything. For if he brought them himself, there is concern that he forged both the witnesses' signatures on the document under discussion and the signatures on the documents he presents to validate it.
from a document against which a challenge was raised and which was upheld in court. That its validity was challenged and the court examined it and confirmed the validity of the witnesses' signatures.
for we do not suspect that the court might err. And validate the document mistakenly, in an incorrect manner.
but we examine the witnesses. We verify that they are valid witnesses and that they indeed give accurate testimony.
and one of them died. After they were satisfied of the validity of the witnesses' signatures, but before they confirmed it in writing.

lest a reader see it and say, 'Two validated it'. For if the two who remain simply write that the document was validated before them and sign, a reader might conclude that the document was validated before two witnesses and not before a court at all.
even if it was written in it, 'In a court'. Even if they wrote, 'We were in a court and this document was validated before us.'

he will say, 'Perhaps they imagined that two constitute a court'. There is still concern that when he sees that only two signed, he will say that the document was validated before only two judges, who mistakenly thought they were a court.

but if it implies that there were three. That it is implied from that document, which says 'in a court', that three were there, for example if it states that the court was appointed to validate the document by a well-known judge who certainly would not have erred in conducting the validation with two (see Rashi, Ketubot 22a).
and they challenged one of them. They challenged the validity of one of the judges involved in validating the document.

that he is a robber or the like. A robber and other transgressors are disqualified from testifying (below 10:4), and just as they are disqualified from testifying, so they are disqualified from judging (below 16:4).
and two others came and testified that he repented. And after his repentance he returns to validity (below 12:4).
if, before they signed, they testified that he repented. If the testimony that he repented was accepted before the other judges signed the validation of the document.
he signs with them, since there were three. For he was valid to judge at that time.

but if after the two signed they testified about him that he repented, he does not sign with them. For he became valid to judge only from the time they testified that he repented, and not before; so it turns out that when the other two judges validated the document, he was not valid to judge with them.
where they challenged him over a transgression. Where they claimed that he was disqualified from judging because of a transgression he committed.
he signs with them, for this is the revealing of a matter that existed earlier. And it became clear that even when they validated the document he was valid to judge with them.
it is permitted to write the validation on the document. To prepare the wording of the document's validation.
and the judges sign after the document has been validated. When the authenticity of the document is established for the judges, they sign the text of the validation.

and the judges need not read the document that they are validating, etc.. For the validation of a document is the court's confirmation that the witnesses' signatures are not forged, and it does not relate to the contents of the document.

a relative may testify to the handwriting of his relative. He confirms that the signature on the document is indeed his relative's signature. Although a relative is disqualified from testifying, nevertheless, since the whole need for validating documents is rabbinic (as explained above 6:1), the Sages qualified these (Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 28a).
and if a third joins them, etc.. For two witnesses are needed for each of the signatures (see below halakhah 3).

and these are among the matters, etc.. Validation of documents is among the matters in which an adult is believed to testify to what he saw as a minor. Although generally a person is not valid to testify to what he saw as a minor, in the validation of documents, which is rabbinic, he is valid (below 14:3, where further matters are detailed in which such witnesses are believed).
on condition that another joins him, etc.. Only when the second witness to the validation of the document recognized their handwriting when he was an adult.
the first said, 'This is my handwriting'. He himself testified to his own signature.
and he and another testified to the handwriting of the second. And in addition he identified and confirmed, together with another witness, the signature of the second witness.

since it turns out that three quarters of the money in the document depends on the testimony of one. For when he says 'This is my handwriting,' half the money is collected on his word, and when he joins another to testify to the second's signature, a further quarter of the money is collected on his word. So three quarters of the money is collected on the word of one witness, yet the Torah said, "on the word of two witnesses shall a matter be established" (Deuteronomy 19:15): half the matter on the word of this one, and half on the word of that one (Rashi, Ketubot 21a).

for three quarters of the money depends on the testimony of relatives. For when the first testifies to his own handwriting, half the money is collected on his word, and when his relative testifies with another to the signature of the second witness, a quarter of the money is collected on his word. So three quarters of the money depends on the testimony of relatives.

and if only one witness is found with this living witness. But it is not possible for the living witness to validate both his own signature and also join another to validate the signature of the second witness, since then three quarters of the money would be collected on his word.

he writes a sample of his signature before witnesses, etc.. He writes a sample of his signature before witnesses and gives the sample to the court, and the witnesses afterwards come to the court and identify and validate his signature on the document.

and he and the other may testify to the handwriting of the deceased. Since he does not need to validate his own signature in court, he is permitted to validate, together with another witness, the signature of the second witness who died.
before they signed. On the validation of the document.

they testify in his presence and he signs. The two judges who recognize the signatures may testify before the third judge to the handwriting of the witnesses signed on the document, and on the basis of their testimony the third judge may sign the validation of the document.

for witnesses may become judges in a matter that is rabbinic. In matters that stem from a rabbinic enactment, such as here in the validation of documents, a person may first be a witness and afterwards judge the same matter.
as we have explained. Above 5:9.
and they do not validate with two. As explained above 6:1; so it turns out that they signed the validation of the document improperly.
but only when all three recognize, etc.. As explained above 6:2.
and they said, 'It is their handwriting,' etc.. They testified that these are indeed the witnesses' signatures, but together with this testified that the testimony in the document is not valid.
they were under duress. They were forced to sign the document against their will.
even though there are other witnesses, etc.. So that there are other ways to validate the document without relying on the testimony of those witnesses who invalidate the document.
whose handwriting appears on a document, etc.. As explained above 6:3.
this one has not been validated. The document is not validated by those means, since the first witnesses invalidate it.
rather, the two on the document are left, etc.. And due to the doubt, the money is left in its presumptive possession.
and he comes to testify to his handwriting in court. To testify that this is indeed his signature and thereby validate the document, as explained above 6:2.

for a person does not testify to his handwriting as such, but testifies to the money in the document. For the essence of the document is the testimony contained in it, and when other witnesses validate the document they give force to the testimony of the witnesses signed on it. But if the document's own witnesses come to validate their signature without remembering the testimony, the validation has no meaning (Sha'arei Yosher 7:9).

but if he did not remember, he may not testify. For in this case his testimony is not based on his memory but on what is written in the document, as though testifying on the basis of the testimony of another (below halakhah 5).
even if the second witness who testified with him reminded him. The one signed with him on the document.

if he remembered, he may testify. Although one might have said that we should not rely on the reminder of the other witness, since he has some interest in the matter, in that it is convenient for him that his words be believed.

because this appears to the litigant as though he testified for him falsely about something he did not know. For there is concern that the claimant misled him and caused him to think that he remembered the testimony even though he did not.
if the claimant was a Torah scholar, etc.. We rely on his care to remind the witness without misleading him or putting words in his mouth.
since this is so. That even the witness himself may not validate the document unless he remembers the event itself, as explained above halakhah 1.
and he is like a shard. Like a broken piece of pottery, which is of no use.
but if their handwriting appears... they validate the document. As explained above 6:2-3.
lest they have retracted. And for some reason wish to annul the document.
and as if they had said, 'We were minors,' ... that they are not believed. As explained above 3:6.

for this is similar only to, etc.. Just as it is obvious that he may not testify to something he heard from another without having been a witness to it (below 17:1), so he may not testify to something he found written in his own handwriting but does not remember at all.
there are ten kinds of disqualification. The laws of each of these disqualified persons are detailed later in this chapter and in chapters 10-16.
the tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it is not apparent whether he is male or female.
and the androgynos. One who has both male and female sexual organs.
because they are possibly women. See Hilchot Ishut 2:24-25.
to make him liable for a sin on his testimony. To make him liable to punishment.
slaves. Canaanite slaves.
just as his brother is a freeborn son. One who has a lineage.
so too the witness must be a freeborn son. Therefore a slave, who has no lineage (for the relationship between a slave and his offspring has no legal meaning), is disqualified from testifying.
slaves, who are obligated in some commandments. Who are obligated in the commandments like women (Hilchot Chagigah 2:1).
one who is half slave and half free. For example, one who was owned by two partners and one of them freed his share (see Hilchot Avadim 7:4).
and anyone who was freed but still lacks a bill of manumission. For example, where his master declared him ownerless but had not yet given him a bill of release (see Hilchot Avadim 8:13).

and he immerses and becomes part of the members of the covenant. For when a slave is freed he must immerse for the sake of conversion, and then his conversion is complete and he becomes like an Israelite (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 13:12).
as we explained in Hilchot Ishut. 2:10-12.
until he brings forth two hairs. Until two hairs grow in the pubic area.
after thirteen full years. After he has completed thirteen years.
and one of the signs of a saris appears in him. That he has one of the signs of a saris (for details of the signs of a saris see Hilchot Ishut 2:13).
until the majority of his years. Until the age of thirty-five, when he is in any case considered an adult.
who has reached the full number of his years. That he is thirteen years old or more.
on whom signs of maturity appeared above. That he has a beard.

he does not need examination. There is no need to examine him to see whether he has brought forth two hairs, because the presumption is that if he has signs of maturity above, he also has signs of maturity below (Hilchot Ishut 2:15).
his testimony is not valid testimony regarding land, because he is not careful with details. And testimony about land requires great precision (Radbaz; and compare Hilchot Mechirah 29:12).
because he is not obligated in the commandments. And one who is not obligated in the commandments is disqualified from testifying, as explained above halakhah 4.
nor an insane person who walks about naked and breaks vessels, etc.. Not only one who behaves insanely in everything, but even one who is insane in just one matter.
the epileptic. One who suffers from the falling sickness (epilepsy).
the epileptic from time to time. Who has a seizure at regular intervals.
and one must deliberate at length over the testimony of epileptics. Because they are sometimes insane and sometimes sensible, one must take time and ascertain their state at that time.
the extremely simple-minded. Whose intellectual level is low.
who do not recognize things that contradict each other. They cannot distinguish between contradictory things that every sensible person can distinguish.

and likewise the panicky, the hasty of mind, and the extremely deranged. Those who are hasty and rash in their interpretation of the reality before them, and who act in an extreme manner, from outbursts and without judgment.
for it is impossible to fix the degrees of intelligence in writing. Fixed rules cannot be set on this matter.
the deaf-mute. One who neither hears nor speaks.

and likewise a deaf person who speaks but does not hear, etc.. A deaf-mute lacking mental capacity is one who neither hears nor speaks (Hilchot Ishut 2:26). However, for testimony it is not enough that a person be of sound mind; he must be able to speak and hear, and if one of these is lacking, he is disqualified from testifying.
must testify in court by his mouth. See above 3:4.
and the warning that they give him. Below 17:2.
became mute. One who was born hearing and speaking and later became mute due to illness.

even if he was examined in the way that they examine for divorce documents. Even though they examined him as they examine a husband who became mute and for whom they wish to give a divorce to his wife, asking him questions three times and seeing whether he knows how to answer them properly by nodding his head (Hilchot Gerushin 2:16).
except for the testimony of a woman. To testify to a woman that her husband died.
because in the case of an agunah they were lenient. To accept even those disqualified from testifying, so that she not remain chained (see ibid. 13:29).
the blind. Those who cannot see.
who recognize the voice and know the people. They know how to distinguish between people by hearing their voices.

from tradition they learned: "Do not put a wicked man as a witness". According to the tradition of the Sages, the verse (Exodus 23:1) is interpreted not only as forbidding cooperation with a wicked person to give false testimony (to be 'a witness of violence'), but as forbidding accepting the testimony of a wicked person in any case ('do not put a wicked man as a witness').
put his hand. Joined.

and knows that the second witness with him is a false witness. Who knows that the second witness did not see the event at all, and that when he testifies that he saw it he is testifying falsely (see below 17:1).
a transgression for which one is liable to lashes. As its parameters are explained in Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1-2.
for one liable to the death penalty of the court. As detailed in Hilchot Sanhedrin 15:10-13.
that he is disqualified. From testifying, since he is wicked.
disqualified by Torah law... disqualified by their rabbinic enactment. See below 11:6, where the difference between disqualification by Torah law and by rabbinic law is explained.
ate the meat of an animal in milk, etc.. For all of which one is liable to lashes by Torah law.
whether for appetite. To satisfy his craving.
or to defy. Out of contempt and rebellion against God's commandments.
shua. Joining wool and linen by mixing and pressing them together.
tavui. Joining by spinning them into a single thread.
nuz. Joining by weaving them into a single fabric.
ate the meat of a bird in milk. Which is prohibited only by rabbinic enactment (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 9:4).
who wore a woolen garment in which a linen thread was lost. And it is uncertain whether it remains there, so the prohibition is only rabbinic (Lechem Mishneh, and see Hilchot Kilayim 10:27).
and we have already enumerated. In Hilchot Sanhedrin chapter 19.
even though they are liable to pay and not liable to lashes. Although they are not punished with lashes, but only pay money.
since they take money that is not theirs through violence. Through wickedness and injustice.
thieves. Those who steal in secret.
and robbers. Those who seize by force, openly.
even if he returned it. For he does not return to validity unless it becomes clear that he repented fully (below 12:4).
a conspiring witness. One who was shown by witnesses to have testified falsely, and is punished with what he intended to do through his testimony (below 18:1).

even if he was proven conspiring in monetary testimony. Not only a conspiring witness who sought to make the defendant liable to death or lashes is disqualified from testifying, as he is a wicked person whose punishment is death or lashes, but also one who testified falsely to make the defendant liable for money is disqualified.
and he paid. Even if they punished him and he paid the money he conspired to make the other liable for, he nevertheless does not return to validity until it becomes clear that he repented fully.
even if he was proven conspiring only after some days. For his disqualification dates from the time he testified falsely, even if the matter became clear at a later time.
both the borrower and the lender are disqualified. For the prohibition of lending at interest applies both to the borrower and to the lender (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 4:2).
fixed interest. Interest that was set in advance at the time of the loan, which is prohibited by Torah law (ibid. 6:1).
the dust of interest. Interest that is prohibited by rabbinic enactment.
small livestock. Small animals, such as sheep.
large livestock. Large animals, such as oxen.
of their own. But one who herds the animals of others is not disqualified, as he does not sin by letting them graze in others' fields when he himself gains nothing from it.

and those who raise small livestock in the Land of Israel are disqualified. Even if they do not graze them in fields but only raise them in their courtyards, they are disqualified, for it is forbidden to raise small livestock in the Land of Israel near fields and vineyards because they stray and graze in the fields of others (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:1-2).
tax collectors. Who bought from the king the right to collect taxes in that place.
because they are presumed to take more than the amount fixed for them by the law of the kingdom. Since the money goes into their own pockets (see also Hilchot Gezelah 5:9).
collectors of the king's portion. Those responsible on behalf of the king for collecting his taxes.
are by default valid. Since their pay is fixed, they are presumed not to collect more than the fixed tax (see also ibid. halakhot 11-12).
those who let pigeons fly. Who release trained pigeons so that they bring with them pigeons from the dovecotes of others (Hilchot Gezelah 6:7).
in a settled area. Within the settlement where the dovecotes of others are found. But in a wilderness or ownerless place, it is permitted.

who sit idle, and when the Sabbatical year comes, etc.. Who trade in produce only in the Sabbatical year, and therefore they are presumed to violate the prohibition of trading in Sabbatical produce. But if they always trade in produce, it can be assumed that it is from the yield of previous years.
one who plays with dice. Who plays gambling games.

presumed to be living off the dice. Even if we did not see him play for money, he is nevertheless presumed to gamble for money (Kesef Mishneh). Some explain that even one who plays for money is not considered a full robber to be disqualified from testifying, and only if he is extremely flawed, having no other trade and making his living from gambling, is he disqualified (Lechem Mishneh).
for it is the dust of robbery. For one who wins money from his fellow in gambling has in his hand the dust of robbery (Hilchot Gezelah 6:10).
they did not say pigeons only. Not only one who gambles in pigeon races is disqualified (Kesef Mishneh, and see Hilchot Gezelah 6:10).
those who wager. Gamblers.
a sharecropper. A laborer who works the field in return for a share of the crop.
who took a small thing, etc.. Who permitted himself to take a little produce while working, though he is not entitled to it.
and not in the way of the land. Whose dealings with people lack gentleness and courtesy (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kiddushin 1:10).
testimony is not entrusted to them. We do not invite him to be present at an event so that he can testify to it.
and testimony is not accepted from them. If he comes to court to testify.
and anyone who accepts testimony, etc.. Any judge who accepts testimony from an am ha'aretz and collects money on its basis.
and they are not careful about false testimony. For even if it becomes clear and known that they testified falsely, they do not care (Rashi, Kiddushin 40b).
those who eat the charity of gentiles in public, etc.. For it is forbidden to take charity from gentiles in public when it can be received discreetly (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:9).
so as not to destroy the people's benefit. For they relied on him as a witness to their dealings, and if his testimony were invalidated, they would suffer a loss.

one witness is believed regarding prohibitions, etc.. He is believed to testify to the permissibility of a thing, such as to testify that a food is permitted to eat or that an object is pure, even if he is a wicked person who is disqualified from testifying.

for a wicked person in a transgression who slaughtered, his slaughter is valid. For it is presumed of every Israelite that if he has the possibility of doing something permissibly he will not choose the way of the prohibition (see Hilchot Shechitah 4:15).
but he is believed regarding that of others. For he is presumed not to sin when he gains nothing from it.
he has. It is permitted to him.

an am ha'aretz is believed to say, 'The produce of so-and-so has been tithed'. Even though an am ha'aretz is not believed about himself to say that his own produce has been tithed (see Hilchot Ma'aserot 9:1).
because the fear of prohibitions is upon the wicked, etc.. And therefore when they have no monetary interest, they are trusted.
the kings of Israel do not testify and none testify against them. But the kings of the house of David do testify, and others testify against them (Hilchot Melachim 3:7).
for they are presumed to be strong and powerful, etc.. And there could be a loss to religion if he does not wish to accept their ruling (ibid.).
and he may testify to the king... as we explained. Above 1:3.
informers. Those who hand over an Israelite or his property to a gentile or a violent person (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:12).
and the epikorsim. Those who deny a connection between the Creator and His creations, and those who deny the Torah (see ibid. halakhah 8, Hilchot Rotzeach 4:10).
and the minim. Those who worship idols, and those who deny the fundamentals of faith in the Creator (see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:7, Hilchot Rotzeach 4:10).
and the meshumadim. Those who transgress God's commandments willfully and in rebellion, even one who commits a single transgression to defy (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:9, Hilchot Rotzeach 4:10).
for the gentiles are neither lifted up nor brought down. If they fell into a pit, we do not rescue them, but neither do we throw them into a pit to cause their death.
and their pious ones have a share in the World to Come. See Hilchot Melachim 8:11.

and these are brought down and not lifted up. It is even a commandment to cause their death, because they oppress Israel and turn them away from God (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:1; and see also Hilchot Rotzeach 4:10-11).
anyone disqualified through a transgression. One disqualified from testifying because he committed a transgression for which one is liable to lashes (as explained above 10:2).

even if they did not warn him, since he is not flogged, etc.. Even if he was not warned about the transgression, and therefore is not liable to lashes, he is nevertheless disqualified from testifying.
who transgresses something that the doer is likely to be unwitting about. Who committed a prohibition regarding which it is reasonable to say that he did not know it is forbidden.
they must warn him. That the thing he is about to do is forbidden.
they must inform him that this is desecration of the Sabbath. That tying and untying are full labors that are forbidden to do on the Sabbath.

perhaps he forgot. For although most people know the prohibition of labor on the Sabbath and festivals, forgetting is common, and it is possible that he forgot that that day is the Sabbath or a festival.
one who always plays with dice. Who plays gambling games all his days and does not engage in the settlement of the world.
or one who became a tax collector. Who bought from the king the right to collect the tax, and is presumed to collect more than he is due.
or a collector who adds for himself. Who is responsible on behalf of the king for collecting the tax, and took more than he was due.
for one who does this is disqualified from testifying. For all of these are disqualified from testifying by rabbinic enactment, as explained above 10:4.

a person is not disqualified for a transgression on the basis of his own word. On the basis of his own admission that he committed a transgression. Nevertheless, ideally he should not be designated as a witness (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 2:3).

borrowed with interest. In the printed editions it reads "the lender with interest," and that is also the meaning of the version here (see Shilat's note in the Rambam Meduyak and the Yalkut Shinuyei Nusach in Frankel's edition).

even though he pays on his own word. And he must return what he stole or robbed, or the interest he took, on the basis of his own testimony, since in monetary payments a litigant's admission is considered full testimony.
and Levi testified and said, 'He lent me with interest'. He joined the testimony of Simon that Reuben lent with interest, and said that he was the borrower.
even though Levi admitted that he borrowed with interest. And since a person does not make himself wicked, one might have said that his testimony is not testimony at all.

and he is believed about Reuben but not believed about himself. We split his statement, and believe his testimony that Reuben lent with interest, but do not believe his testimony that he was the borrower.
that so-and-so had relations with him. In the manner of a male homosexual act.

whether willingly. Even when he testified that the act was done with his consent, we believe his testimony that so-and-so committed the prohibition, although we do not believe his testimony that he himself was a partner to the transgression.

to kill him but not to kill her. Since a person is close to his wife and is not believed about her, we split his statement and believe his words that so-and-so committed the prohibition of adultery, but do not believe his words that the prohibition was with his wife.
he and another join to put him to death. The one who committed the act.
for a person is not close to his property. And therefore we believe his words even regarding the ox.
who repented and turned back, or who was flogged, is valid. For when he repents and turns from his deeds, or is flogged, he returns to validity, as explained in the following halakhot.
this one is possibly disqualified. For there is conflicting testimony about his validity.

therefore he may not testify, etc.. For due to the doubt, money is left in the presumptive possession of its owner (and the presumption of the money's ownership takes precedence over the presumption of the witness's validity).
and he may not judge. For one disqualified from testifying is also disqualified from judging (below 16:4).
until it is known that he repented. Then even if he had been disqualified, he returns to validity.
once he was flogged by the court, he returns to his validity. See also Hilchot Sanhedrin 17:7.
even though they paid, they need repentance, etc.. It is not enough that they returned the money, but they must repent in a way that makes clear that they have turned from their evil deeds.
until they tear up their documents. So that he cannot collect even the principal as a lender with a document, but only as an oral lender (Sema, section 34, subsection 73).
even to a gentile. Although by the basic law it is permitted to lend to a gentile with interest (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 5:1).
those who play with dice. Those who play gambling games.
their pieces. Their game pieces.
even for free. Although playing for nothing does not violate the prohibition of the dust of robbery (see above 10:4).
those who let pigeons fly. Who release trained pigeons so that they bring with them pigeons from the dovecotes of others.
that they not do so even in the wilderness. Although in the wilderness there is no prohibition against releasing pigeons, but only in a settled place (above 10:4).
and they shall be examined. And it will become clear that they no longer trade in Sabbatical produce.
and not mere words of retraction. Not just a declaration that they will stop trading in that produce.
I gathered two hundred zuz from Sabbatical produce. I earned from the forbidden trade in Sabbatical produce.

and they are given as a gift to the poor. For they are the main beneficiaries of the ownerless status of produce in the Sabbatical year, so the main loss from trading in produce is caused to them (Yad Ramah, Sanhedrin 25b).
one who is faithless regarding oaths. One suspected of swearing falsely (see above halakhah 1).
a butcher. A slaughterer.
who used to examine for himself. The animals, to make sure they were not likely to die from a wound they had and were not terefot.
and a terefah came out from under his hand. He sold terefah meat to the market.

for he is among those who eat terefah. Since he sold terefah to others, he is presumed not to refrain from eating terefot himself (Kesef Mishneh); some explain that since we see that he caused others to stumble in eating terefot for monetary gain, we suspect that he would also give false testimony for monetary gain, and he is disqualified from testifying just as those who eat terefah are disqualified (Arukh HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 34:7, and see Piskei VeShitot).

and let him go to a place where they do not know him, etc.. For when he returns a valuable lost item there, or loses a large sum of money there because of his animal that he slaughtered and turned out to be terefah, it is evident that he repented fully and is no longer eager for money (see also Hilchot Shechitah there, Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 8:9).
significant money. A large sum of money.
disqualified from testimony. To testify for each other.
from tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
on the word of sons. On the basis of their testimony.
and brothers from the father. Even if they are not brothers from the mother.
and their sons with one another. First cousins.

and needless to say an uncle with his nephew. Whose closeness is greater than that of two first cousins. For all the relationship derives from the head of the family, and the uncle is closer to him than a cousin is.
other relatives from the mother. For example, an uncle with his sister's son.
by way of marriage. That the relationship was created through marriage ties, for example a father with his son-in-law, the husband of his daughter.
converts. Who were related in their gentile state.
are not subject to the law of relatives. They are not judged as relatives.
for a convert who converted is like a newborn child. And has no connection to his relatives from when he was a gentile (see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:11).
they are first to first. Their relationship is called 'first to first,' since they are both first from the father from whom the relationship derives.
and their sons with one another, second to second. The relationship of cousins is called 'second to second,' since they are both second from the grandfather from whom the relationship derives.
and the sons of their sons with one another. For example, Pinchas son of Elazar son of Aaron with Jonathan son of Gershom son of Moses.
third to first is valid. For example, Pinchas son of Elazar son of Aaron is valid to testify for Moses.

and needless to say third to second. For example, Pinchas son of Elazar son of Aaron is valid to testify for Gershom son of Moses, since the relationship derives from the head of the family, and so the relationship of third to second is more remote than third to first.
second to second. First cousins with one another.
second to first. An uncle with his brother's son.
therefore a father with his son's son is disqualified. Because it is like second to first.
to whom you are related. For example, your father's sister.
except for the husband of his father's mother. A step-grandfather, since the disqualification of relationship was applied only to a stepfather or stepson and not beyond that.
whom you are related to. For example, your father's brothers.
any two women who are second to second to each other. For example, female cousins.

their husbands may testify for each other. Because the relationship of the husbands to each other derives from the fact that a husband is like his wife, and one does not say 'a husband is like his wife' twice in the distant relationship of second to second.
but if they were first to first... they may not testify for each other. Because in a close relationship one does say 'a husband is like his wife' twice.
and likewise he may not testify for his wife's sister's son. For his relationship to him is first to second.
nor for the husband of his wife's sister's daughter. Because in the relationship of first to second one says twice 'a husband is like his wife.'
but he may testify for the son of the husband of his wife's sister whom he had by another woman. For he is not related to him, as he is the stepson of his wife's sister.
you may testify for his other relatives. For there is no relationship between them at all, as in halakhah 12 below (Kesef Mishneh).
such as his son. Whom he has by another woman.
not for her son... nor for her daughter. Who were born to her from another man.
even though the marriage has not yet been completed. That he has not yet brought her into the chuppah.
she is like a married woman regarding testimony. And he is disqualified from testifying for her, because he has already drawn close to her in his mind.
but if he testified for the relatives of his betrothed... they do not disqualify them. Since he has not yet drawn close in his mind to her relatives (Kesef Mishneh).
therefore a friend and an enemy are valid for testimony. As explained below 16:6.
even though he is disqualified from judging. As explained in Hilchot Sanhedrin 23:6.

because he is the husband of your relative. For the disqualification from testifying arises from a marital connection. Just as a person is disqualified from testifying for his female relative, so he is disqualified for her husband (above 13:6).
one who knew testimony for his fellow, etc.. Who saw the event at a time when he was valid to testify, and afterwards, before he came to testify, became disqualified.
his son-in-law. The husband of his daughter.
one who can hear. Who hears with his ears.
one who can see. Who sees with his eyes.
even though he can measure the land that he testifies about and specify its boundaries. That despite his blindness he can define the size of the area and state its borders.

this is the rule: anyone who is valid at the beginning and valid at the end is valid. For the testimony to be accepted, he must be valid to testify both at the time of seeing the event and at the time of testifying in court.

at the beginning disqualified, even though at the end valid, is disqualified. And all the more so one who was valid at the beginning and disqualified at the end is disqualified, since at the time of testifying he may not testify.

since they are matters of their own enactment. For by basic Torah law this testimony is not required at all, and since only the Sages required it, they were lenient to accept it even when it began in disqualification because he was a minor.
this is the handwriting of my father or my brother. To identify their signatures on a document, and thereby validate the document and give it force.

because validation of documents is rabbinic. For the Sages enacted both the signing of witnesses on the document and the way to validate and confirm the witnesses' signatures, and therefore they did not require here valid testimony by Torah law (see above 3:4, 6:1).

and she was given the customs of virgins. That the customs observed at the weddings of virgins were observed at her wedding, such as that she covered herself with a veil that was customarily worn at their weddings only by virgins. Consequently she is entitled to a ketubah of two hundred dinars, and is not like a widow, who is entitled only to one hundred (Hilchot Ishut 10:7).

that this place is a beit ha-peras. A beit ha-peras is a place where a grave was plowed over and the bones scattered through the field, and the Sages decreed that the area of a hundred cubits by a hundred cubits from the place of the grave is impure (see Hilchot Tumat Met 2:16, 10:1). Since this impurity is rabbinic, when it was known that there was a beit ha-peras in that area, a minor is believed to testify that the impure area is in a particular place and that the rest of the area is pure (Kesef Mishneh in the name of the Ran).
up to here we came on the Sabbath. That this is the end of the Sabbath boundary.

for reducing the boundary to two thousand only is rabbinic. For by Torah law it is permitted to go out up to twelve mil (see Hilchot Shabbat 27:1), and the Sages are the ones who limited the boundary to two thousand cubits only, and therefore we rely on his words regarding this boundary.
to immerse and eat of his terumah. So that he may eat terumah in purity (see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 20:15).
who used to divide terumah with us. Who used to receive with us, the priests, a share of the terumah from the field.
by his own hand. He is believed when he testifies that he himself was sent to carry priestly gifts (but if he testified that others used to bring him priestly gifts, he is not believed).

and my father said to me, 'This family is valid, this family is disqualified'. That it was known that one family was disqualified from terumah, and the witness testified which of the families it is (Kesef Mishneh in the name of the Ran).

and we ate at the cutting-off of so-and-so, etc.. It was the custom that a family one of whose members married a disqualified woman would break a barrel of fruit in the town square and announce that so-and-so had been cut off from their family.
for all these things, to establish this priest to eat terumah, are rabbinic, etc.. For the obligation of terumah nowadays is not from the Torah but rabbinic (Hilchot Terumot 1:26).
one who knew testimony for his fellow before he became a robber. Who signed a document dated before the time he became disqualified from testifying.

he may not testify to his handwriting. He is not permitted to validate the document, since he is disqualified from testifying. And others too may not validate it, for they suspect that he forged the document after he became disqualified and wrote an earlier date in it.
but if his handwriting was established, etc.. If the court saw the document signed before that witness became disqualified from testifying.
this is a valid document. For it became clear that the document was written while he was valid.
and likewise if he became his son-in-law. And before that he signed a document that concerned his father-in-law.
he may not testify to his handwriting. He is not permitted to validate the document, since he is disqualified from testifying because of his relationship.
but others may testify, etc.. The document may be validated even though there is no explicit knowledge that it was signed by him before he became disqualified.

for one disqualified through a transgression is suspected of forgery. Whereas one disqualified through relationship is not suspected of forging the date on the document and writing an earlier date than the time he became disqualified.
that has only two witnesses, etc.. But if it had many witnesses, the testimony is established through the remaining witnesses (as explained above 5:6).

even though he delivered the document to him before two valid witnesses. And in principle a document delivered before witnesses is valid even if no witnesses are signed on it (see for example Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:2).
because it is forged from within. And therefore it has no force at all.
one who writes all his property to two people on the testimony of one. Who wrote, 'All my property is given as a gift to so-and-so and to so-and-so.'
the document is invalid. And even the person from whom the witnesses are not disqualified gains nothing.

for these are two testimonies even though they are in one document. For he gave different properties to different people, and the matter is considered two testimonies (Kesef Mishneh). Some explained that since he separated the gifts into two ('that I gave... and that I gave'), there is a separate testimony for each of the gifts (Machaneh Ephraim, Edut 3).

to what is this comparable? To one who says, 'Be witnesses for me that I gave, etc.'. In this case it is clear that the testimonies are separate, since each testimony relates to a different act, and so too in the case in the previous paragraph each testimony relates to a separate gift, and therefore they are two separate testimonies.
like testifying for himself. For his own benefit.
to challenge them regarding the bathhouse, etc.. To challenge the public's ownership of these properties.
in the plaza of a city. A large public square.
none of the townspeople may testify, etc.. For he is a partner in public property, and it is like testifying for himself.

until he removes himself from it by an act of acquisition. Until he renounces his share in the public property under discussion and gives this force by a kinyan sudar (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
since it is made for hearing. For hearing the reading of the Torah from it on Sabbaths and festivals.
for it is impossible for a person to remove himself from it. For he needs to hear the reading in it.
one who says, 'Give a maneh to the poor of my city'. A sick man who commanded before his death to give a maneh to the poor and died, and now the heirs are being sued for it.

the judges of that city may not judge, etc.. For they have an interest in the testimony, since it is convenient for them that the maneh be given to the poor, which reduces the townspeople's obligation to support them.
even if two of the townspeople said, etc.. Even if they undertook to pay the poor fund in any case, and so have no interest in the testimony.
for it is a benefit to them that these poor people become wealthy, etc.. So that they will not need to support them in coming years.
land that is between two partners. That is owned by two partners.
and a claimant came to remove it from the hand of the partner. Claiming that the partner's share of the land belongs to him.
he may not testify for his partner about it. For if the partner loses his share, they will have to share the remainder together, so the testimony concerns him.
unless he removed himself from it, etc.. He renounced his share in the partnership and gave this force by a kinyan sudar.

and that if his creditor came and seized it from the hand of the partner, he pays him its value. And he even accepted upon himself that if his creditor comes, and he has no money to pay him, and because of this the creditor collects the land from the partner, he will afterwards pay the partner the value of the field. For otherwise he still has an interest, since it is convenient for him to leave the land in his partner's hand so that his creditor can collect from him.
the challenger of the field. One who claims it is his.
the sharecropper. A sharecropper, a person who works the field for its owner in return for a share of the crop.
but the renter. Of the field for a fixed sum each year.
if he took the rent in his hand, etc.. If he has not yet paid the rent, and announces that he will give the rent to whoever is proven to be the owner of the field.
for if the field goes to the challenger. And he prevails in the case.

he must give him the rent for all the years he sat in it. For when it turns out that the renter paid someone who is not the owner of the field, the law is that he pays again to the true owner and sues the one who rented him a field that was not his (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 16:8). Therefore if the renter has paid, he has an interest and cannot testify.
and Judah came to challenge Simon the borrower and remove land from his hand. Claiming that it is his.
if Simon has another field against the debt. If he has another field from which the lender can collect.
then Reuben the guarantor may testify, etc.. For he has no interest, since even if they take the field from Simon, they will collect from him only from Simon's other field.

and likewise the first buyer may testify for the second buyer, etc.. When two bought fields from the seller one after the other, the first buyer may testify for the second buyer that the field is his.

on condition that the seller has a freehold field, etc.. On condition that the seller has another field in his possession. Then the first buyer has no interest, since even if they remove the field from his possession (on the claim that the seller robbed it and it was never his), he can return to the seller and collect from him. Whereas when the seller has no field, it is convenient for the first buyer to leave the second buyer's field in his possession so that he can return and collect it from him.

for Simon wants to leave this field and this garment in Reuben's hand, etc.. Simon wants the field or the garment to be in Reuben's possession, so that afterwards he can take them from him on a claim of robbery.

for it is possible that Simon's proof is stronger, etc.. For example, both Simon and Judah have witnesses that the field is theirs, and so it is convenient for Simon that the field not remain in Judah's hand but in Reuben's.
perhaps he finds it easier to take it from Levi. For example, if Judah is a difficult litigant and Simon prefers not to go to court with him.
he sold the stolen garment to Levi. And Simon despaired of it.
Simon testifies about it that it is not Judah's. And he has no interest, for in any case he cannot claim back his stolen item.

for the buyer already acquired it through despair and change of possession. For when a person steals an item from his fellow and sells it to another person and the victim despairs of the item, the buyer acquires the item and need not return it to the victim (Hilchot Gezelah 2:3).

and Reuben the robber has already died and has nothing from which to collect its value. Although in a case of despair and change of possession the robber must return to the victim the value of the stolen item, since he died and the stolen item is not in his heirs' hands, they are not obligated to pay the value of the stolen item (see ibid. 5:5, and see Piskei VeShitot).
and he shall pay him its value. For he cannot claim the garment itself since Levi already acquired it, but he can claim its value from the robber.
because in the end, if it remains in the heir's hand, it will return to him. Since the garment's passing to his heirs is not considered a change of possession.
without guarantee. Where he explicitly stipulated that if it is taken from him he need not compensate him.

for he wants it to remain in Simon's hand so that Reuben's creditor will come and seize it for his debt. Reuben wants the field to be in Simon's possession so that if Reuben cannot pay his debt, his creditor can collect from Simon the field that Reuben sold him, which is mortgaged to the creditor.

and he shall not be a wicked borrower who does not pay. That he not be in the category of a wicked person who borrows and does not repay (based on Psalms 37:21, and see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 1:3). However, regarding the buyer he is not considered wicked, since he explicitly stipulated that he sells him the field without guarantee (Kesef Mishneh).
and it is rare. Uncommon, not usual.
Reuben testifies for him about it, etc.. For he gains nothing by its remaining in Simon's hand.

for even if it remained in Simon's hand, Reuben's creditor does not seize from movable property. For a creditor does not collect movables from buyers from the debtor (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 18:2).

even if they were pledged. A pledged property is one on which it was agreed in advance that the creditor would collect his debt from it (ibid. halakhah 3). And even where they agreed so in advance, since these are movables, if he sold them to another person the creditor cannot collect his debt from them (see ibid. halakhah 5).
where Simon admitted that this cow and garment belong to Reuben. And that Judah is claiming them unlawfully.
Simon returns and claims money from Reuben. He will claim from him the return of the money he paid him.

perhaps he transferred them to his creditor and wrote to him 'that I will acquire,' etc.. For when a person writes in the loan document that he transfers to his creditor, together with land, the right to collect from all the property he will acquire in the future ('that I will acquire'), so that he can collect from them, the lien applies even to movables, and the creditor can collect from them even if they were sold to another person (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 18:2).
two who are related to each other are not ordained to the Sanhedrin. Two relatives are not appointed to judge together.
in the Great Sanhedrin. The Great Court in Jerusalem of seventy-one judges.
in the Lesser Sanhedrin. A municipal court of twenty-three judges (and even in a court of three, two relatives do not judge together, Kesef Mishneh).
